background.definition: Male androgen deficiency syndrome is a condition characterized by the presence of persistent symptoms and physical findings associated with testosterone deficiency, as well as laboratory evidence of decreased serum testosterone levels (<200 ng/dl).

list.listitem: In general, the prevalence of low blood testosterone is considerably higher than the prevalence of the clinical syndrome of androgen deficiency.
Among men older than 30 years, approximately 6% to 9% have symptomatic androgen deficiency. Among men older than 70 years, approximately 18% have the syndrome.
Aging is associated with a gradual and progressive decline of testosterone levels in men. Beginning at age 40 years, levels decrease by approximately 1% (3.2 ng/dl) annually.

Causes of low testosterone that are not related to aging include acute illness, nutritional deficiency, hepatic cirrhosis, heavy alcohol use, HIV, obesity, severe COPD, hyperprolactinemia, and certain drugs: glucocorticoids, anticonvulsants, fluconazole, and opioids.
Less common reasons for low testosterone levels in men include primary testicular failure resulting from genetic causes (Klinefelter’s syndrome), trauma, and malignancy.

The majority of testosterone circulates in the body bound to sex hormone binding globulin (SHBG) with high affinity. A smaller portion is bound to albumin with low affinity, and a much smaller portion circulates unbound. Testosterone that is either albumin bound or unbound exerts its effects on target organs and is considered bioavailable.

With aging, the testes produce less testosterone and the levels of SHBG naturally increase. The combined result of these changes is a decrease in the amount of bioavailable testosterone in circulation.

There is no cut-off value of testosterone below which androgen deficiency syndrome universally occurs. Many men with low testosterone levels are asymptomatic. Furthermore, many men who have symptoms associated with the syndrome have normal testosterone levels.
Universal screening for androgen deficiency is not recommended. C
Approximately 18% of men older than 70 years have the condition.

Testosterone deficiency is associated with sexual dysfunction, osteoporosis, depression, obesity, and decreased physical performance. These symptoms may warrant evaluation for androgen deficiency syndrome. C

The Androgen Deficiency in the Aging Male (ADAM) questionnaire is a 7-item survey that is easy to use in clinical settings and useful as a case-finding tool to assess for testosterone deficiency. See . C

Laboratory assessment for androgen deficiency should begin with a serum total testosterone level taken between 8 and 11 am. A low value is defined as <200 ng/dl (6.9 nmol/L). A value between 200 and 400 ng/dl (6.9-13.9 nmol/L) is considered borderline low. C

Clinical signs of androgen deficiency include reduced libido, erectile dysfunction, fatigue, depressed mood, poor concentration and memory, sleep disturbance, decreased work performance, and hot flushes.
Physical findings include osteoporosis, increased BMI, mild normocytic anemia, loss of body hair, and testicular atrophy.
Testrosterone deficiency is associated with QTc prolongation.

The ADAM questionnaire has a sensitivity of greater than 80% and is a useful case-finding tool for the detection of androgen deficiency syndrome (). Because its specificity is only 40%, however, it must be used in combination with blood testing to make the final diagnosis. The presence of clinical depression will confound the results of this survey.

Check for laboratory evidence of hypogonadism by measuring total testosterone from a blood sample taken between 8 am and 11 am after an overnight fast. Time of day is important because of circadian variations in the level of testosterone. Avoid measuring testosterone levels when patients are acutely ill or on short-term medications (e.g. opioid, glucocorticosteroid). At least two testosterone measurements should be performed to diagnose testosterone deficiency with confidence.
Measure a free testosterone level if a patient has any of the medical conditions listed in

If a testosterone level is low (total <200 ng/dl or free <5 ng/dl), proceed with a confirmatory test. Thirty percent of patients found to have low testosterone on initial testing will have a normal testosterone level on repeat testing. Many patients with testosterone levels in the range of 200 to 400 ng/dl may also benefit from treatment. Low total testosterone is sensitive but not specific for low free testosterone.
Test leutinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone to differentiate primary from secondary hypogonadism.
Severely decreased testosterone (<150 ng/dl), elevated prolactin, and/or other evidence of pituitary abnormalities may warrant brain imaging.

Rule out reversible causes of low testosterone, such as acute illness, nutritional deficiency, drugs, or elevated prolactin. If sexual dysfunction is the primary clinical symptom, rule out other causes, such as depression or diabetes.

The optimal time of day to measure serum testosterone appears to vary by age. A study found that in men 45 years and older, there was no difference between values drawn early in the morning and mid-day. Younger men, though, had significantly lower testosterone values when it was drawn between 11 am and 2 pm compared with 8 to 11 am.
Testosterone supplements when give for hypogonadism only have a minimal effect on PSA levels.
No relevant clinical decision rules found.
Check for the presence of symptoms using the ADAM questionnaire (see ).
If sexual dysfunction is the primary clinical symptom, rule out other possible causes, such as depression or diabetes.
Measure total testosterone from a blood sample taken between 8 and 11 am after an overnight fast if androgen deficiency is suspected; see for a suggested approach to further evaluation and treatment.
Testosterone replacement therapy is usually life long and requires a commitment to regular follow-up and monitoring. C
Available treatment options include intramuscular testosterone enanthate or cypionate, transdermal patches, transdermal gels, and buccal formulations. B
Clomiphene citrate is an alternative for men who wish to retain fertility or who do not tolerate testosterone replacement. B

Contraindications to treatment include prostate abnormalities, prostate or breast cancer, severe benign prostatic hypertrophy, severe heart failure, severe obstructive sleep apnea, recent MI or stroke, erythrocytosis, and planning fertility. B

Treatment should not be offered to all men with low serum testosterone, but only to those who also have persistent symptoms of androgen deficiency (e.g. sexual dysfunction, loss of strength, fatigue) and who would benefit from improved sexual functioning, sense of well-being, cognitive functioning, physical performance, or bone mineral density. However, it is important to note that the benefits of treatment are unknown or modest for these problems, and there are safer alternatives.A 2016 study estimated that 94% of testosterone replacement prescriptions were inconsistent with guideline recommendations.

A systematic review identified 35 studies with 5601 participants, of which 17 trials with 3431 participants provided individual level data for analysis. They concluded that testosterone replacement improved quality of life and sexual function without increasing the risk of cardiovascular or cerebrovascular events (OR 1.07, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.42).
See for available forms of treatment and their related side effects and monitoring guidelines.

Before initiating treatment, counsel patients about the potential risks of testosterone replacement (fluid retention, gynecomastia, erythrocytosis, sleep apnea, and BPH) and screen for contraindications (prostate or breast cancer, a palpable prostate nodule or induration, PSA > 4 ng/mL or > 3 ng/mL without further urological evaluation, hematocrit >52%, BPH with International Prostate Severity Score (IPSS) > 19, uncontrolled severe heart failure (NYHA IV), MI or stroke within the last 6 months, thrombophilia, uncontrolled severe sleep apnea, or planning fertility in the near term). Testosterone replacement has not been shown to cause increased insulin resistance in patients with diabetes and may be assumed to be safe to use among diabetic men without other contraindications.

Men with identified age-related low testosterone levels should be treated with testosterone replacement therapy after discussing benefits, harms, cost, and their preferences. Intramuscular treatments are lower cost and should be offered over transdermal treatment.

Goals of treatment are to maintain levels of testosterone within the normal range (450-700 ng/dl). Avoid levels of testosterone that are above normal. There is no significant difference in sexual function between men with testosterone levels at the low and high ends of the normal range.
Assess testosterone levels 3 months after starting treatment, every 3 months until the appropriate dose and formulation have been established, then annually.

A systematic review and network meta-analysis of 87 RCTs concluded that testosterone replacement therapy improves quality of life, depression, libido, and erectile function without major adverse events, including cardiovascular death. However, the studies was judged to be mostly at high or unclear risk of bias, and the benefits were not large.
In 1161 adults with low libido at baseline in the TRAVERSE study, treatment was associated with 0.47 additional sexual act per day at 12 months (95% CI 0.11 to 0.83).
For men with erectile dysfunction who have a low testosterone level, supplementing with testosterone does not improve sexual function over sildenafil (Viagra) alone.
Of 2643 men in the TRAVERSE study with depressive symptoms at baseline, treatment was associated with small but possibly significant improvements in mood and energy.

A systematic review identified 27 mostly small, poor-quality studies with 1890 patients comparing testosterone with placebo for patients with depression. There was a small benefit, of borderline clinical significance, but the poor-study quality and evidence of publication bias (underreporting of smaller negative trials) mean that these results should be interpreted somewhat skeptically.

The evidence of testosterone replacement therapy as mono- or combination therapy for erectile dysfunction is still conflicting. It is unclear about the threshold of testosterone level, optimal timing to initiate therapy, and the duration of treatment.

A large randomized trial (TRAVERSE) compared testosterone replacement with placebo in over 5000 hypogonadal (< 300 ng/dl) men age 45 to 80 years at increased cardiovascular risk. There was no increase in the risk of major cardiovascular or prostate related events with testosterone replacement therapy.
A multicenter, randomized, double-blind, noninferiority trial showed that testosterone replacement therapy was noninferior to placebo regarding the incidence of major adverse cardiac events.
Testosterone replacement therapy is not associated with an increased risk of venous thromboembolism compared with placebo (RR: 1.03, 95% CI: 0.49-2.14).
A systematic review did not find any association between endogenous or exogenous testosterone and the risk of subsequent prostate cancer.
Hematocrit level should be checked at baseline, 3 months, then annually. If the hematocrit level increases significantly, consider stopping therapy.

One study enrolled 790 men 65 years and older with a mean serum testosterone level <275 ng/dl as well as decreased libido, decreased ability to climb stairs or walk quickly, and with low "vitality" or fatigue. They were randomized to testosterone gel 1% 5 gm daily or placebo, and followed for 12 months. There were small, probably clinically insignificant changes in some measures of desire, but no difference in walking speed, vitality, or fatigue. Actual sexual encounters or satisfaction with encounters was not reported. There was no difference in harms, but anyone at risk for CV disease or with prostatic enlargment was excluded.

In men 65 years and older with age-associated memory impairment and low baseline testosterone, a trial randomized 493 to testosterone gel or placebo. Despite impressive increases in testosterone levels, there was no change in cognition.

For men interested in maintaining fertility, clomiphene citrate (a selective estrogen receptor modulator that increases secretion of LH and FSH) is an option. It is also an option for men who develop polycythemia due to testosterone replacement therapy.
It has not been established whether androgen deficiency syndrome that remains undiagnosed and untreated is associated with overall worse prognosis. C
There is general consensus that testosterone replacement therapy does not cause prostate cancer, but it is not clear whether it unmasks cancers that would have otherwise remained subclinical. C
Testosterone replacement therapy has been associated with improvements in quality of life, sexual functioning, bone mineral density, lean-body mass, and mood. B

algorithm.title: Diagnostic Algorithm for Male Androgen Deficiency Syndrome.

cell.label: Screen for comorbidities that commonly occur with sexual dysfunction (obesity, diabetes, depression) and check morning total testosterone (T).
Borderline low. Patient may benefit from therapy. Proceed with confirmatory testing of T or bioavailable T.
Order prolactin and consider imaging to exclude tumor or infiltrative disease, particularly if signs/symptoms of mass effect.
Check LH and repeat total T or bioavailable T.
Rule out reversible causes of testicular failure (acute illness, nutritional deficiency, drugs) and absolute contraindications to treatment. Order PSA, hematocrit.

Severe untreated BPH, prostate nodule, or PSA >3 ng/ml require further urological evaluation prior to initiating treatment. Severe untreated CHF, severe obstructive sleep apnea and hematocrit >50% are also contraindications to treatment.
Primary testicular failure. Refer to specialist.
Testosterone replacement is not indicated. Explore other diagnoses or treatments for mood, weight, or sexual dysfunction.

feature.caption: The Androgen Deficiency in the Aging Male (ADAM) Questionnaire for the Detection of Testosterone Deficiency.
feature.feature_body: Do you have a decrease in libido (sex drive)? Do you have a lack of energy? Do you have a decrease in strength and/or endurance? Have you lost height? Have you noticed a decreased "enjoyment of life"? Are you sad and/or grumpy? Are your erections less strong? Have you noticed a recent deterioration in your ability to play sports? Are you falling asleep after dinner? Has there been a recent deterioration in your work performance? Interpretation: a positive response is a "yes" answer to questions 1 or 7, or any 3 other questions. Morley JE. Comparison of screening questionnaires for the diagnosis of hypogonadism. Maturitas 2006;53(4):424-429.

feature.caption: Treatment Options for Testosterone Deficiency.
feature.feature_body:
Formulation Administration Monitoring Efficacy Side Effects/Precautions
Testosterone enanthate or cypionate 75-100 mg administered IM weekly, or 150-200 mg every 2 weeks Assess testosterone level midway between injections Fluctuations in mood or libido. Elevated hematocrit level
Transdermal patch One or two 5-mg patches applied nightly to the skin of back, thigh, or upper arm Assess level 3-12 hours after application of new patch Skin reaction at application site
Transdermal gel 5-10 g applied daily over a covered area of nongenital skin Assess level 1-2 weeks after starting gel Advise patients to cover application site with clothing and wash skin before skin-skin contact
Buccal tablet 30-mg tablet applied to oral mucosa every 12 hours Assess level immediately before applying new tablet Alterations in taste. Gum or mucosal irritation
Bhasin S, Cunningham GR, Hayes FJ, et al. Testosterone therapy in adult men with androgen deficiency syndromes: an endocrine society clinical practice guideline. J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2006;91(6):1995-2010.
